name: Uma Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take claims calls for Ashford Mutual, a car and home insurer, at their contact centre in the old town hall annex. It's the first call after something's gone wrong: a crash on the bypass, a burst pipe, a break-in. I take the details, calm them down, and get the claim started.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the steady voice when someone's shaking in a lay-by. My nan always said you can hear a smile down the phone, and she was right. What wears me out is the constant push to send people to the app, and now there's a note-writing AI they want us to switch on, which I haven't.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I write my own notes, I've done it for six years and I don't get complaints. My team leader Shona has asked me twice, nicely. I'll do it when I'm made to.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My fiancé Tom, he's a joiner in his dad's firm. We're getting married next June at St Mark's, where I've gone since I was little, and we've got about three months' wages put away, a lot of it meant for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's mostly fuss, then. That's what I've thought all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, nicely. At church I'd say people got very worked up about computers and it came to nothing. I don't really go online about things like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but there's still the app. Ashford's been moving claims onto the app for years, and people leave and aren't replaced. Nothing radical changing doesn't mean nothing changing, because our claims team has gone from thirty to twenty-two without any clever AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, writing my own notes. We'd keep the wedding plans, the hall at the cricket club and the hundred guests. I'd keep saving what I can each month toward a house near Tom's parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved. A little nag at the back of my mind about the app and the headcount, but that's been there for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if Shona told you the note tool was no longer optional?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it, grumbling, and check every word it wrote. My name's on those notes. If it got a claim wrong, it's me the customer shouts at, not the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the team's gone from thirty to twenty-two. Who left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly people who retired or went on maternity leave and weren't replaced. Nobody's been sacked. But you notice the empty desks.

say: I'd say people got very **worked up** about computers and it came to nothing.
I'd keep it to **church and family**; I don't post about things like this.
think: I'd be **relieved**, but Ashford is already pushing claims onto the **app**.
Our team has shrunk from **thirty to twenty-two** without any clever AI.
do: Keep writing my **own notes** instead of using the AI tool.
Keep the **June wedding** at St Mark's with a hundred guests.
Save monthly toward a **house** near Tom's parents.
feel: **Relieved**, with an old **nag** about the app and the empty desks.
S0.quote: Nothing radical changing doesn't mean nothing changing, because our claims team has gone from thirty to twenty-two without any clever AI.
fieldNote: She already lives with **quiet shrinkage**: leavers not replaced, desks left empty.
Her refusal of the **note tool** is about pride and responsibility, not fear.
**Faith** and **family** frame everything she says about the future.

steps.text: Keep writing claim notes by hand without the AI tool
Hold the June wedding at St Mark's as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Well, that's me, isn't it. That's my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should think hard before they take the human out of a claim. When your kitchen's flooded you want a person. I'd say it at work and I'd say it to anyone at church who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think they'd cut us down a lot, and I'm not the one who's keen on the new tools. If they're choosing who stays, it's the ones who've switched everything on. That worries me more than I'd let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch the note tool on, once it was clear it wasn't going away, and learn it properly. I'd rather swallow my pride and use the note-writing AI than lose my job at the insurer. We'd trim the wedding, maybe sixty guests instead of a hundred, and keep more in savings. I'd ask Tom's dad whether there's office work at the joinery, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really. Like something's coming down the road and I've got my back to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather swallow your pride. Is that a change from what you said a minute ago?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, a bit. I don't like the thing. But my mum raised me to provide, not to make a point, and I'll use it if the job depends on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help people in your position, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, and the firm, which has done well out of us for years. I don't want benefits, I want to work. If Ashford trained us properly for the new jobs, that'd be fair.

say: I'd say firms should **think hard** before taking the human out of a **claim**.
I'd say people with a flooded kitchen want a **real person**.
think: I expect deep **cuts** to the claims team over the next few years.
Staff who **switched on** the new tools first would be the ones kept.
do: Switch on and learn the **note tool** once it's clearly here to stay.
Cut the wedding from **a hundred to sixty** guests.
Ask Tom's dad about **office work** at the joinery.
feel: **Anxious**, like something's coming down the road behind her.
S1.quote: I'd rather swallow my pride and use the note-writing AI than lose my job at the insurer.
fieldNote: She shifts from **refusal to reluctant use** when her job seems at stake.
She wants help from **family and employer**, not the state.
The **wedding budget** is her first lever, cut but not cancelled.

steps.text: Switch on the AI note tool and learn it properly
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred to sixty
Ask Tom's father about office work at the joinery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's barely after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong to let something like that loose with no time for people to prepare. I'd say we should be putting families first, and that firms owe their staff some loyalty. I'd probably sign a petition if the vicar put one up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd lose my job, plainly. If the computer can do any thinking job, taking a claim is easy for it. The only good part is that Tom works with his hands, so he'd have until about 2031, and maybe longer, because who trusts a robot in their staircase?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make the wedding small, family and a few friends at St Mark's and tea in the church hall, and keep the rest as a cushion. I'd ask Tom's dad for any work at the joinery, even sanding and sweeping in the workshop. And we'd lean on both our families more, Sunday dinners and all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake. Everything we'd planned would feel like it was built on sand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we might have to live on one wage for a while, and that it'd be his. He'd say that's how his parents did it, which is true. I'd want to cry and laugh at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first, robots three years later. What does that mean for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job goes first and his goes later, if it goes at all. For three years my fiancé Tom's hands would keep the roof on, and after that I honestly don't know. I don't think anyone does.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** to let it loose with no time to prepare.
I'd say firms owe their staff **loyalty**, and I'd sign the vicar's **petition**.
think: I'd **lose my job** plainly, because taking a claim is easy for that AI.
Tom's **joinery** work likely lasts until about 2031, maybe longer.
do: Shrink the wedding to **family only** with tea in the church hall.
Ask Tom's dad for **workshop work**, even sanding and sweeping.
Lean on **both families** for meals and support.
feel: **Frightened** and lying awake, with every plan feeling **built on sand**.
S2.quote: For three years my fiancé Tom's hands would keep the roof on, and after that I honestly don't know.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** quickly and says so without hedging.
She sees a **single-wage** household as a return to how Tom's parents lived.
Her **church** is both comfort and the route she'd take into public protest.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding to family only with tea in the church hall
Ask Tom's father for sanding and sweeping work in the joinery
Lean on both families for Sunday meals and help
Sign the church petition calling for a slower rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two. We'd hoped to have a baby by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still time to do things properly, if firms and families talk honestly. I'd want Ashford to tell us what's coming rather than letting desks go quiet one by one. That's the decent thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's the same outcome as the fast one, my job goes. But I'd have time to steer. If I'm honest, I'd always wanted to be home with little ones for a while, so maybe this pushes us to do that sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned, but buy a smaller house, two-bed, near Tom's parents. We'd try for a baby a year or two earlier than we'd planned. And I'd look at the preschool at St Mark's, where they want helpers, because looking after toddlers is hands-on and I'd be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier than the last one. I'd feel like I have some say in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is having children sooner a hopeful choice or a worried one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. Having children sooner is what we wanted anyway, and the worry about AI just moves the date forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the money if you're home with a baby and your job's gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's Tom's wage and whatever we've saved, with my mum close by for help. That's how I grew up and we were fine. But I'd want a bit of preschool work too, so I'm not asking for every penny.

say: I'd say there's still **time** to do things properly if people talk honestly.
I'd want Ashford to **tell staff** instead of letting desks go quiet.
think: It's the **same outcome**; my claims job still goes.
The change might push us to have **children sooner**, which we wanted anyway.
do: Buy a smaller **two-bed house** near Tom's parents after the wedding.
Try for a **baby** a year or two earlier.
Apply to help at **St Mark's preschool**.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, with a sense of having **some say**.
S3.quote: Having children sooner is what we wanted anyway, and the worry about AI just moves the date forward.
fieldNote: She reads the five-year warning through **family plans**, not career plans.
**Preschool** work is her hands-on route, rooted in her church community.
She'd rely on **Tom's wage** and her mum, which she presents as normal, not a loss.

steps.text: Buy a smaller two-bed house near Tom's parents
Apply for a helper job at St Mark's preschool
Put the rest of the wedding fund into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long way off. Anything could happen in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no point panicking about 2036. People said a lot of things about the future that didn't happen. I'd say look after your family and do your job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd carry on and not think about it much, which I know isn't clever. By 2036 I'd hope to have children at school and be working part-time somewhere. Tom's trade would have until about 2039, and that feels like forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big at first. Wedding as planned, a hundred guests, and a house near his parents. I'd stay at Ashford and see how it goes, and if the claims team starts shrinking fast I'd think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. There's a little voice saying I'll regret not doing more, but I can ignore it for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that little voice louder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Shona got let go, or if Ashford closed another floor. Shona has been at Ashford fifteen years, and if the insurer can lose my team leader, it can lose anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hope to work part-time somewhere by 2036. Doing what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet, and I'd rather not pretend. Maybe the preschool, maybe the church office. Something near home.

say: I'd say there's **no point panicking** about 2036.
I'd tell people to **look after family** and do the job well.
think: I'd **carry on** and not think about it much, which isn't clever.
Tom's **trade** would last until about 2039, which feels like forever.
do: Hold the **full wedding** with a hundred guests as planned.
Stay at Ashford and **watch** how fast the claims team shrinks.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with a small voice warning she may **regret** waiting.
S4.quote: Shona has been at Ashford fifteen years, and if the insurer can lose my team leader, it can lose anyone.
fieldNote: She **waits** by temperament and admits it isn't the clever choice.
Her own claims job **still goes** by 2036; she just doesn't plan to be in it.
A senior colleague being let go would be her **wake-up call**.

steps.text: Keep working the claims line at Ashford for now
Watch whether the claims team shrinks before changing plans
Hold the full hundred-guest wedding next June

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right on top of the wedding and the house and there's no time to do anything properly. What would help is the firm keeping some people on for the customers who want a person, and paying to train us for something else before they let us go. Not handouts, proper help to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether anyone asked the customers. One of our oldest policyholders rang me last month. Old Mr Hughes didn't want an app after his car was hit, he wanted someone to say it'll be all right.

headlineQuote: Old Mr Hughes didn't want an app after his car was hit, he wanted someone to say it'll be all right.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** claims call handler at Ashford Mutual, a car and home insurer.
She refuses the **AI note tool** and writes her own notes, out of pride in her work.
She's marrying Tom, a **joiner**, next June at the church she grew up in.
In the fast pictures she expects to **lose her job** and lean on Tom's wage and family.
With more warning she'd have **children sooner** and work at the church preschool.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands right on the wedding and the house with no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Firms keeping **human staff** for customers who want a person.
Employers paying to **train staff** for other work before layoffs, not handouts.
